goNow: Call 911 or go to the hospital now for swallowed chemicals, pesticides, cleaning fluids or too many tablets
Sleepy, confused, fits, trouble breathing or vomiting
Burns around the mouth or smell of chemicals
Any swallowed button battery or magnet

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Poisons can be swallowed, breathed in or touched. Common ones at home are medicines, cleaning fluids, pesticides, petrol, and carbon monoxide. Do not give salt water or milk, and do not make the person vomit unless a poison expert says so. Bring the container.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Vomiting, tummy pain
Drowsiness, confusion
Burns on lips
Odd smell on the breath
Trouble breathing
Fits

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Call 911 or the UP-PGH National Poison Management and Control Center
Take the person away from fumes into fresh air
Wash skin with water if chemicals touched the skin
Rinse eyes for 15 minutes
Keep the container and bring it
Do not induce vomiting

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Keep medicines and chemicals out of reach, in their own bottles
Never put chemicals in drink bottles
Use pesticides with gloves and keep children away
Check gas stoves and heaters have air

topics.title: Nosebleed
short: Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes.
Most nosebleeds stop by themselves.
Do not tilt the head back.
goNow: Bleeding that does not stop after 20 minutes of pinching
A nosebleed after a hard hit to the head, or with fainting
Heavy bleeding in someone who takes blood thinners
Frequent nosebleeds in a child

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: The inside of the nose has many small vessels near the surface, and they bleed easily. Dry air, picking, colds and allergies are common causes. High blood pressure can make a nosebleed last longer.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Blood from one or both nostrils
A taste of blood in the throat

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Sit up and lean forward
Pinch the soft part of the nose just below the bone for 10 minutes without letting go
Breathe through the mouth
Spit out blood, do not swallow
Do not blow the nose for several hours

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Do not pick the nose
Keep the nose moist with a little petroleum jelly
Treat allergies and colds
Keep blood pressure in check

topics.title: Fainting
short: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness, often from low blood flow to the brain.
Lay the person down and raise the legs.
Most faints are harmless, but some are not.
goNow: Fainting with chest pain, a racing or very slow heartbeat, or trouble breathing
Fainting during exercise or with no warning
A fall with a head injury, or a person who does not wake within a minute or two
Weakness of one side, trouble speaking, or a bad headache

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Fainting often follows standing too long, heat, pain, fear, dehydration or standing up fast. Heart problems can also cause it, which is why a first faint should be checked by a doctor.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Feeling dizzy, hot or sick first
Vision grey or dim
Sweating, pale
Falling down

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Lay the person flat and raise the legs
Loosen tight clothes
Check that they are breathing
Do not give water until awake
Let them get up slowly
If not awake in a minute or breathing is poor, call 911

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Drink enough fluid
Get up slowly
Do not stand too long in heat
Review medicines with a doctor if you faint

topics.title: Electric shock
short: Turn off the power before you touch the person.
Call 911, even if they look fine.
Electric shock can upset the heartbeat hours later.
goNow: Anyone who was shocked and is unconscious, not breathing, or has burns: call 911
A shock from a high voltage line or lightning
Chest pain, irregular heartbeat or trouble breathing
A shock to a pregnant woman or a child

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Electric current can burn the skin and also harm the heart. The skin burn is often small but the damage inside can be bigger. Never touch a person who is still in contact with the current. For a plug or house wiring: turn off the main switch, or push the person away with dry wood. For a fallen power line: stay at least 10 metres away, never touch the person or the wire, and call 911 and the power company.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Burns where the current went in and out
Muscle pain
Fast or uneven heartbeat
Confusion
Fainting

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Turn off the main switch or unplug
If you cannot, push the person away with a dry, non-metal object such as wood
Call 911
Check breathing and start CPR if needed
Cool burns with running water
Always get a medical check
For a fallen power line: stay at least 10 metres away and call 911 and the power company

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Keep wires, sockets and appliances in good repair
Keep water away from electrics
Cover sockets near children
Stay indoors in a lightning storm and away from tall trees

topics.title: Eye injury
short: Do not rub the eye.
Rinse with clean water for 15 minutes if chemicals splashed into it.
Eye injuries need a doctor right away.
goNow: A chemical splash in the eye: rinse for 15 minutes and go to the hospital
Something stuck in the eye, a cut eye or a hard blow to the eye
Loss of vision, seeing flashes, or double vision
Blood in the clear part of the eye or eye that looks different

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: The eye is easily damaged by chemicals, flying objects and blows. Rubbing can make a scratch worse. A speck in the eye can often be washed out. Anything deeper needs a doctor.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Pain, redness, watering
Blurred vision
Light hurts
Feeling of something in the eye

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Wash your hands first
Rinse the eye with clean running water for 15 minutes for chemicals
Blink many times to move a speck out
Do not rub, and do not use tweezers or cotton buds
Cover loosely and go to the hospital
Do not remove an object stuck in the eye

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Wear safety glasses when cutting, welding or using chemicals
Keep fireworks away from children
Take care with sprays and paint

topics.title: Bee, wasp and jellyfish stings
short: Most stings only hurt and swell for a day or two.
Take out a stinger and cool the spot.
A serious allergy to a sting is an emergency.
goNow: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue, trouble breathing or hives all over: call 911
Dizziness, fainting, a fast pulse or a rapid spread of the rash
Many stings at once, or stings in the mouth or throat
Fever or spreading redness after a few days
A jellyfish sting with severe pain, confusion, trouble breathing or collapse: call 911

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: A sting puts a small amount of venom under the skin. It causes pain, redness and swelling. A few people are allergic and can have a severe reaction within minutes. Jellyfish stings may cause lines of stinging welts.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Sharp pain
A red swelling
Itching
Warmth
A raised bump

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Scrape out the stinger with a flat edge such as a card, do not squeeze it
Wash with soap and water
Put a cold pack on for 10 minutes
Rinse jellyfish stings with vinegar if you have it, or sea water, not fresh water
An antihistamine can help itching
Watch for 30 minutes for a severe reaction
Use an adrenaline pen if prescribed

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Do not swat bees
Keep food and drinks covered outdoors
Wear shoes and long sleeves in bush
Stay out of the sea when jellyfish are around

topics.title: Severe allergic reaction
short: A severe allergy can close the airway in minutes.
Call 911 at once. Use an adrenaline pen if you have one.
Lie down with the legs raised. Do not stand or walk.
goNow: Swelling of the lips, tongue or face, or trouble breathing: call 911 now
Hives with dizziness, fainting, vomiting or a fast, weak pulse
A reaction that follows a sting, food, or new medicine
Tight throat or hoarse voice

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Anaphylaxis is the most serious kind of allergic reaction. Common triggers are food (shrimp, peanuts), medicines (antibiotics, painkillers), and stings. It comes on quickly and can be deadly. Adrenaline is the first treatment, and every person who has had it should carry two pens.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Hives, itching, red skin
Swollen lips, tongue, face
Hard breathing, wheeze
Dizziness, faint
Vomiting, cramps

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Call 911
Use an adrenaline pen on the outer thigh if prescribed
Lay the person flat and raise the legs
If they vomit or struggle to breathe, let them sit or lie on the side
Stay with them until help arrives
A second dose after 5 to 15 minutes if no better

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Know your triggers and read labels
Tell doctors and dentists about allergies
Carry adrenaline and an allergy card if you have one
Wear a medical alert band

topics.title: Head injury
short: Most bumps on the head are minor, but some are serious.
Watch for changes in the first 24 hours.
Do not leave the person alone that night.
goNow: Passing out, a fit, or no waking up easily
Repeated vomiting, a bad headache that grows, or confusion
Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ear, or weakness or numbness
Unequal pupils, or a soft spot on a baby that bulges
Anyone over 65 or on blood thinners (such as warfarin or aspirin) who hit their head, even if they seem fine

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: A blow to the head can bruise the brain (concussion) or cause bleeding inside the skull, which may show hours later. Older people, those on blood thinners and children are at higher risk. Anyone with warning signs needs a doctor now.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Headache, dizziness
Nausea
Confusion or memory gap
Sleepy
Ringing in ears

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Hold a cold pack on a bump for 10 minutes
Rest and avoid screens, sport and alcohol
Paracetamol for pain, not aspirin
Wake a sleeping person once or twice to check they respond
Have another adult watch for 24 hours
Do not drive

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Wear a helmet on bikes and motorbikes
Wear seat belts
Use child seats
Make the home safe against falls

topics.title: Sunburn
short: Sunburn is a burn from too much sun, and it can come hours later.
Cool the skin and drink water.
Blisters or fever mean see a doctor.
goNow: Blisters over a large area, fever or chills, or severe pain
Confusion, dizziness, or faint
Sunburn in a baby under one year

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Strong sun damages skin. Ultraviolet (UV) rays are strongest between 10 am and 4 pm. Repeated burns raise the risk of skin cancer and wrinkles later.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Red, sore skin
Heat and tightness
Blisters
Peeling after a few days

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Get out of the sun
Cool shower or damp cloths
Aloe vera or plain moisturiser
Drink extra water
Paracetamol for pain
Do not pop blisters

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Wear a hat, long sleeves and sunglasses
Sunscreen SPF 30 or more, put on again every 2 hours
Stay in shade at noon
Keep babies out of direct sun

topics.title: Flood and typhoon health safety
short: Floodwater can carry germs, sharp things and live wires.
Stay out of it. If you wade, wash well after.
Cover cuts, and know the signs of leptospirosis.
goNow: Fever, muscle pain or red eyes within 2 weeks of wading in floodwater: see a doctor, tell them about the flood
Diarrhoea with weakness or dehydration
Trouble breathing, chest pain, or injuries
Anyone trapped by rising water: call 911

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: After floods, illnesses such as leptospirosis, diarrhoea, typhoid, dengue and skin infections rise. Drinking water may be unsafe. Wires, sharp objects and open drains are other dangers. Make a go-bag before storm season.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Fever after a flood
Muscle pain
Red eyes
Yellow skin
Loose stools
Skin rash

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Stay out of floodwater, wear boots if you must go in
Wash with soap and clean water after
Boil drinking water for 1 minute or use clean bottled water
Keep medicines, papers and a flashlight in a waterproof bag
Cover cuts
Doxycycline prevention may be offered by the health centre, ask there

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Know the evacuation centre
Keep a go-bag ready
Clear drains and standing water
Keep a phone charged

topics.title: Anemia (low blood)
short: Anemia means your blood does not carry enough oxygen around the body.
You may feel tired, weak, dizzy or look pale.
Common causes are too little iron, blood loss or long-term illness. A blood test finds out which.
goNow: Chest pain, a racing heart or fainting
Very short of breath when resting
Black or bloody stools, or vomiting blood

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Red blood cells carry oxygen. In anemia you have too few of them, or too little of the part that carries oxygen. The most common cause is not enough iron. Heavy periods, bleeding in the gut, pregnancy and some long-term illnesses can also cause it.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Feeling tired and weak
Pale skin, lips or inside of the eyelids
Dizziness or headache
Cold hands and feet
Short of breath on small effort

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
See a doctor for a blood test before taking iron on your own
Take iron tablets exactly as your doctor says
Eat iron-rich food such as liver, lean meat, fish, eggs, malunggay and dark leafy greens
Vitamin C food such as calamansi or guava helps the body use iron
Tea and coffee with meals can block iron

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Eat a mix of foods with iron
Pregnant women should have prenatal check-ups
Treat worms and heavy bleeding early
Ask a doctor about heavy periods

topics.title: Violence at home
short: Being hurt, scared or controlled by someone at home is never your fault.
Help is free and private in the Philippines.
You can ask for help even if you are not ready to leave.
goNow: You or someone else is in danger right now: call 911
A serious injury, or a threat to kill
A child is being hurt

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Domestic violence is when a partner or family member hurts, threatens, shames or controls another person. It can be hitting, but also words, money control or forcing sex. It happens to women, men, children and older people. In the Philippines the law protects women and children, and barangay and police desks can help.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Injuries that do not match the story
Being afraid of a partner or family member
Not allowed to see friends or hold money
Children who are scared, quiet or hurt

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Tell a person you trust
Keep a bag with ID, money and medicines where you can grab it
Know the nearest barangay VAW desk or police women's desk
Call 911 in danger
Ask a doctor or health worker for a check, they can keep notes

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Talk about problems early
Ask for help from a counsellor or the barangay
Teach children that no one may hurt them

topics.title: Abuse of older people
short: Older people can be hurt, scared, robbed of money or left without care.
It is often done by someone they know.
Telling someone you trust is the first step.
goNow: Someone is in danger right now: call 911
A serious injury, or an older person who is not eating, drinking or getting medicine

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Elder abuse is harm to an older adult by someone who should care for them. It can be hitting, shouting, shaming, taking money or property, or leaving them without food, medicine or help. Older people who depend on others, or who are forgetful, are at higher risk.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.text:
Bruises or injuries with no clear reason
Fear of one person
Sudden changes in money, bank or property
Dirty clothes, weight loss or missed medicine
Staying alone for long hours

sections.heading: What helps at home
sections.text:
Visit often and talk privately with the older person
Share the work of caring so no one is worn out
Report to the barangay, the police or the DSWD
See a doctor, who can check and record injuries

sections.heading: Prevent it
sections.text:
Support carers with rest and help
Keep papers and bank cards safe
Stay in touch with neighbours and family
